```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-studio-brief">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The task</p>
<ol class="lx-studio-task">
<li><b>Produce:</b> an audit note on a study that weighs cost against carbon: each flaw, its fix and its effect, then the corrected conclusion with the condition it rests on.</li>
<li><b>From:</b> a fictional study of 40 electric buses, its tables, and your browser's recomputation of every number after each fix.</li>
<li><b>Done when:</b> the rubric's bar for Consistent accounting and for Realism: one boundary, the emissions question named, who pays named, inputs' evidence status and a list of what is left out.</li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-hint">About 35 minutes guided here, then about 90 minutes on your own:</p>
<ul class="lx-hint">
<li>pick a study from your field: a report, a paper or a press release;</li>
<li>run the checklist under Self-check on it;</li>
<li>recompute one number it rests on, on one boundary;</li>
<li>write the audit note and rate it against the rubric.</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="lx-interactive lx-cards" data-learn="r07-cost-carbon-properly" data-src="../assets/learn/data/r07-cost-carbon-properly.json ../assets/learn/data/path.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- r07-task:start (written from the data file by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The study (fictional)</p>
<p><b>Electric buses for Port Alder: cheaper and carbon-free</b>. R. Okonjo and L. Varga, Harbourline Consulting (fictional), report to Port Alder Transit (fictional), 2026.</p>
<p>Replacing Port Alder Transit's 40 oldest diesel buses with battery-electric buses saves $1.15 million a year and cuts the fleet's CO₂ by 100%.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Its inputs (illustrative)</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts r07-in"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Input</th><th scope="col">Electric</th><th scope="col">Diesel</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Price per bus</th><td data-l="Electric">$1,000,000 + $60,000 charger</td><td data-l="Diesel">$560,000</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Energy per mile</th><td data-l="Electric">2.2 kWh, at the depot meter, charging losses included</td><td data-l="Diesel">3.5 mpg (the 2009 buses)</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Energy price</th><td data-l="Electric">$0.09 per kWh, energy rate only</td><td data-l="Diesel">$3.60 per gallon</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Repairs per mile</th><td data-l="Electric">$0.60</td><td data-l="Diesel">$1.20 (the 2009 buses)</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Purchase credit</th><td data-l="Electric">$150,000 per bus, the state's clean-bus credit (fictional)</td><td data-l="Diesel">none</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="lx-hint">Both fleets: 40 buses, 36,000 miles each a year, a 12-year life, a 3% real discount rate.</p><p class="r07-plan"><b>From Port Alder Transit's fleet plan (fictional):</b> The 40 buses bought in 2009 retire in 2026; 40 new diesel buses replace them (4.5 mpg, $0.85 a mile in repairs) unless the board funds another option.</p><p class="lx-hint">Units: t is a metric tonne (1,000 kg); mpg is miles per U.S. gallon; a demand charge is dollars per kW of the month's highest draw (a kW-month), billed each month.</p><details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Two numbers worked from these inputs</summary><ul><li>Charging energy: 40 buses × 36,000 miles × 2.2 kWh per mile = 3,168 MWh a year; at $0.09 per kWh, $285,120 a year.</li><li>Diesel fuel, as the study runs it: 1,440,000 miles ÷ 3.5 mpg = 411,429 gallons a year; at $3.60 per gallon, $1,481,143 a year.</li></ul></details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Four flaws, each fixed, and the conclusion after each</summary><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Fix</th><th scope="col">What it changes</th><th scope="col">Saving a year, electric against diesel</th><th scope="col">Attributed CO₂ cut</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>The study as published</td><td>none</td><td>$1.15 million</td><td>4,192 t (100%)</td></tr>
<tr><td>One boundary</td><td>One boundary: charging 3,168 MWh a year at 0.366 t per MWh is attributed 1,160 t. The CO₂ cut falls from 100% to 72%.</td><td>$1.15 million</td><td>3,033 t (72%)</td></tr>
<tr><td>A fair baseline</td><td>Fair baseline: new diesel buses burn 320,000 gallons a year, not 411,429. Diesel's yearly cost falls by $0.83 million.</td><td>$0.32 million</td><td>2,101 t (64%)</td></tr>
<tr><td>Grid costs</td><td>Grid costs: $288,000 a year in demand charges, and $1.80 million up front for the depot ($180,832 a year as an annual equivalent).</td><td>−0.15 million</td><td>2,101 t (64%)</td></tr>
<tr><td>The credit once</td><td>The credit once: the $6.00 million stays off the price up front; the second count, $500,000 a year, goes.</td><td>−0.65 million</td><td>2,101 t (64%)</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div></details>
<p><b>Audited:</b> Electric costs $0.65 million a year more and lowers attributed CO₂ by 2,101 t (64%): about $309 per attributed tonne. That is for the transit agency, with charging at EIA's 2023 U.S. average factor.</p>
<!-- r07-task:end -->
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you find each flaw, fix it and watch the conclusion change; your note stays in this browser.</p>

The U.S. grid emitted 1.53 billion tonnes over 4.18 trillion kWh generated in 2023 (EIA): 0.366 t per MWh.</span></p>
<p class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><span><b>Up front and a year.</b> One-time costs become a yearly equivalent with the <span class="lx-term" data-term="capital-recovery-factor">capital recovery factor</span> at 3% over 12 years, 0.1005 (<a href="a01-project-tea.html">A1</a>).</span></p>
```

## Two notes on the same study, and who pays
:::

```{=html}
<div id="r07-exemplars" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- r07-exemplars:start (written from the data file by LX.Exemplars' staticHTML in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-ex-cols">
<div class="lx-ex-ans weak"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Weak note · Developing</p><p class="lx-ex-lines"><b>Audit:</b> the study looks optimistic [1]. Electric buses still have no emissions [2], but costs are probably higher [3]. More research is needed. [4]</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Falls short:</b> No flaw is named, so no one can check or fix it.</li><li value="2"><b>Falls short:</b> True at the tailpipe only; the power plants that charge them emit.</li><li value="3"><b>Falls short:</b> No number, no baseline, no 'whose cost'.</li><li value="4"><b>Falls short:</b> It says nothing a reader could act on.</li></ol></div>
<div class="lx-ex-ans good"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Strong note · Proficient</p><p class="lx-ex-lines"><b>Boundary:</b> charging is in the cost but its CO₂ is not; at EIA's 2023 U.S. average factor, the electric fleet is attributed 1,160 t a year. [1]
<b>Baseline:</b> without the project the agency buys new diesel buses (4.5 mpg), not the 2009 fleet (3.5 mpg). [2]
<b>Grid:</b> add the depot connection ($1.80 million up front) and demand charges ($288,000 a year). [3]
<b>Credit:</b> counted once, in the capital line; the second $500,000 a year removed. [4]
<b>Evidence:</b> the prices, miles and 2.2 kWh per mile are the study's illustrative assumptions; the replacement plan is the agency's own document (fictional); the CO₂ factors are EIA's published figures. [5]
<b>Leaves out:</b> making the buses and batteries, street air and noise, grid losses, a grid that gets cleaner, battery replacement. [6]
<b>Conclusion:</b> for the agency, electric costs $0.65 million a year more and lowers attributed CO₂ by 2,101 t (64%), about $309 per tonne, if the grid is at the 2023 U.S. average. [7]</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Works:</b> Names the mismatch, the fix and the factor's source.</li><li value="2"><b>Works:</b> The counterfactual, stated from the agency's own plan.</li><li value="3"><b>Works:</b> Up front and annual kept apart.</li><li value="4"><b>Works:</b> Says which count stays and why.</li><li value="5"><b>Works:</b> Each key input's evidence status, as the Realism bar asks.</li><li value="6"><b>Works:</b> What the audit does not count, said.</li><li value="7"><b>Works:</b> Cost and attributed CO₂ on one boundary, whose cost, and the condition that moves it most.</li></ol></div>
</div>
<table class="lx-facts lx-ex-diff"><thead><tr><th scope="col"></th><th scope="col">Weak note</th><th scope="col">Strong note</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Flaws</th><td>None named</td><td>Four, each with its fix</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Numbers</th><td>None</td><td>Cost, CO₂ and cost per tonne</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Whose cost</th><td>Unsaid</td><td>The agency's, with the credit once</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Conditions</th><td>None</td><td>The grid's CO₂ factor</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Evidence and limits</th><td>None</td><td>Each input's status; what is left out</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Who pays, who gains: the audited plan, a year, against new diesel buses</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Who</th><th scope="col">Cost or change</th><th scope="col">Per attributed tonne of CO₂</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Port Alder Transit<br><span class="lx-hint">the agency's budget</span></th><td>+$0.65 million a year</td><td>$309 per attributed tonne (about)</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">The state<br><span class="lx-hint">pays the credit</span></th><td>$6.00 million up front ($0.60 million a year as an annual equivalent)</td><td>a transfer to the agency</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Agency and state together<br><span class="lx-hint">the credit nets out</span></th><td>+$1.25 million a year</td><td>$595 per attributed tonne (about)</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Attributed CO₂<br><span class="lx-hint">operating energy, charging at EIA's 2023 U.S. grid average</span></th><td>−2,101 t a year</td><td>64% of the diesel fleet's</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Where the audited conclusion holds</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">It holds when</th><th scope="col">It leaves out</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><ul><li>the inputs are this fictional study's, in 2025 dollars, over a 12-year life at 3%;</li><li>costs are the agency's, with the state's credit once; CO₂ is each fleet's operating energy, at the tailpipe or the power plant;</li><li>charging's CO₂ is attributed at the grid's average factor (EIA, 2023): what the grid really emits less needs a consequential analysis (A10);</li><li>2.2 kWh per mile is at the depot meter, charging losses included;</li><li>the agency pays the depot connection; both fleets run the same routes and miles.</li></ul></td><td><ul><li>making the buses and batteries: embodied CO₂ is outside both fleets' counts (a life-cycle boundary, A11);</li><li>grid losses between plant and depot (EIA: about 5%), which would raise charging's CO₂ a little;</li><li>tailpipe air pollution and noise in the streets, which electric buses cut;</li><li>a grid that gets cleaner over the 12 years, and battery replacement;</li><li>federal grants, fuel and power price changes.</li></ul></td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">How far up the ladder is each number?</p><ul><li>The transit board voted the money for 40 electric buses. <b>Funded.</b> Funded: money committed, nothing built yet.</li><li>The utility approved the depot's new service connection. <b>Permitted.</b> Permitted: approved, not yet built; its cost estimate is still an estimate.</li><li>Ten electric buses have carried passengers since March. <b>Operating.</b> Operating: in service, but a few months do not show a year's energy use.</li><li>Over a full year the ten buses used their expected energy per mile, winter included. <b>At design output.</b> At design output: the 2.2 kWh per mile now rests on measured service, not a brochure.</li><li>The audit's cost per attributed tonne of CO₂. <b>Not on the ladder: a projection.</b> A projection: a model's output from inputs on several rungs, not a stage of anything built.</li></ul>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The study against the audit, thousands of 2025 dollars a year (rounded)</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Line</th><th scope="col">Study</th><th scope="col">Audited</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Electric: buses and chargers, net of the credit<br><span class="lx-hint">up front $36.40 million</span></th><td>3,657</td><td>3,657</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Electric: electricity</th><td>285</td><td>285</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Electric: demand charges</th><td>0</td><td>288</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Electric: depot connection<br><span class="lx-hint">up front $1.80 million</span></th><td>0</td><td>181</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Electric: repairs</th><td>864</td><td>864</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Electric: the credit again, as income</th><td>−500</td><td>0</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Electric, total</th><td>4,306</td><td>5,275</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Diesel: buses<br><span class="lx-hint">up front $22.40 million</span></th><td>2,250</td><td>2,250</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Diesel: fuel<br><span class="lx-hint">3.5 then 4.5 miles per gallon</span></th><td>1,481</td><td>1,152</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Diesel: repairs</th><td>1,728</td><td>1,224</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Diesel, total</th><td>5,459</td><td>4,626</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Which grid factor, and which question?</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>The audit counts charging at the grid's average factor: the buses' share of what the plants emit.</li>
<li>What charging changes depends on which plants respond in the hours the buses charge, now and as the grid is built out: <a href="a10-emissions-questions.html">A10</a>'s questions 2 and 3.</li>
<li>Name which question your number answers, and show the result at the other factors, as step 6 does.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this studio leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>A life-cycle boundary: making the buses and their batteries (<a href="a11-lca-nexus.html">A11</a>).</li>
<li>Health and noise in the streets, which electric buses improve.</li>
<li>Uncertainty in each input: <a href="r06-uncertainty-properly.html">R6</a>.</li>
<li>Who pays for a depot connection when a utility recovers it from all its customers: the cost moves, it does not vanish.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

::: {#selfcheck .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## Check your own work against the rubric
:::

```{=html}
<div id="r07-rubric" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- r07-rubric:start (written by LX.Rubric's staticHTML, from the course rubric, and from the data file's checklist, in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts lx-rb-static"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Competence</th><th scope="col">Developing</th><th scope="col">Proficient (the bar)</th><th scope="col">Strong</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Consistent accounting<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: cost and CO₂ for the same service, alternatives and years, the emissions question named (an attributed share or a change in the system), and whose cost each number is.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Costs and emissions on different boundaries.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Cost and emissions on one boundary; emissions question named; who pays and who benefits named.</td><td data-l="Strong">Distributional and environmental side effects estimated with stated assumptions.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Realism<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: each key input with its evidence status, and a list of what the audit leaves out.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Assumes announced projects exist.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Evidence status of key inputs; a 'what the analysis leaves out' list.</td><td data-l="Strong">Realism checked with a practitioner or primary documents.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Cost and carbon, before you trust a result</p>
<ul><li><b>Same service:</b> Both options deliver the same service: the same routes and miles, the same years.</li><li><b>One boundary:</b> Cost and CO₂ cover the same service, alternatives and years; whose costs count and which emissions stages are in are stated, with what is left out.</li><li><b>A stated counterfactual:</b> One sentence says what happens without the project, from a plan or a rule, not a convenient past.</li><li><b>The emissions question:</b> Average or marginal factor, and why: whose share, or what changes.</li><li><b>Grid and connection costs:</b> Upgrades, demand charges and connection fees are priced, with who pays them.</li><li><b>Credits once:</b> Each grant or credit appears in one line, and is a transfer for the state and the agency together.</li><li><b>Up front and annual apart:</b> One-time amounts and their annual equivalents are labelled, with the rate and the life.</li><li><b>The condition that moves it:</b> The input that changes the conclusion most is named, with the result at its other values.</li></ul>
<!-- r07-rubric:end -->
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="r7-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="tailpipe" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A fleet with no tailpipe emits no CO₂.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. At the 2023 U.S. average factor, charging Port Alder's buses is attributed about 1,160 t of CO₂ a year, emitted at power plants.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="credit" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A purchase credit makes a project cheaper for everyone.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It moves money from the state to the agency: the audited buses cost the agency $0.65 million a year more, and the two together $1.25 million.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="baseline" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The fair baseline is the fleet running today.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It is what would happen without the project: here the replacement plan's new diesel buses, not the 2009 ones.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Researcher</span>From this studio to your own study</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><b>Proficient:</b> cost and CO₂ on one boundary, the emissions question named, who pays named, inputs' evidence status and what is left out.</li>
<li><b>Strong goes further:</b> side effects for other people and places, estimated with stated assumptions.</li>
<li><b>To test it:</b> give your note to someone who did not write the study, and ask them to recompute one number.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:ghg"><p>In the reported scenarios, reductions in attributed emissions were on the order of one to two percent of regional totals or less.</p><p>Reductions are computed under average-emission-intensity accounting with perfect foresight; they are not estimates of the consequential (marginal) system response.</p><footer>Approved excerpt of: Li et al. (2025), <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.crsus.2025.100367">Cell Reports Sustainability</a>.</footer></blockquote>
<p class="lx-hint"><b>Reading it.</b> <span class="lx-term" data-term="attributed-emissions">Attributed emissions</span>: a user's share of the grid's CO₂, here at its average intensity, as in this studio's audit.</p>
<p class="lx-hint"><span class="lx-term" data-term="perfect-foresight">Perfect foresight</span>: the model knows the coming hours in advance. <span class="lx-term" data-term="consequential-analysis">Consequential response</span>: how much the grid's own emissions actually change.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Case file <a href="cf6-shifting-load-to-clean-hours.html">CF6</a>: how much shifting load to cleaner hours can cut emissions, and when.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>
<ul>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/environment/emissions/co2_vol_mass.php">Carbon Dioxide Emissions Coefficients</a>, 18 September 2024 (diesel and home heating fuel: 10.19 kg CO₂ per gallon).</li>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=74&amp;t=11">How much carbon dioxide is produced per kilowatthour of U.S. electricity generation?</a> Data for 2023; updated 11 December 2024.</li>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=105&amp;t=3">How much electricity is lost in electricity transmission and distribution in the United States?</a> About 5% in 2018 to 2022; updated 7 November 2023.</li>
<li>ISO 14044:2006, Environmental management: life cycle assessment, requirements and guidelines (functional unit, system boundary, allocation), by name.</li>
<li>Li et al. (2025). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.crsus.2025.100367">Real-time greenhouse gas emission intensity informed demand-side load regulation for power grid decarbonization</a>. Cell Reports Sustainability 2, 100367.</li>
```
